issues.legal_issue: A ruler vested with plenary governing powers could delegate those powers to another person, who could then enact legislation under the delegation.
material_facts: The governing law of the state preserved the ruler’s legislative, executive, and judicial powers and his prerogative to make laws.
The ruler entrusted all his powers and functions concerning the government of the state, including the power to make laws, to the person who later enacted the challenged law.
The delegation remained in force when the challenged law was enacted.
issues.conclusion: The delegate had authority to enact the law, so the challenge to its validity on grounds of lack of legislative competence failed.
issues.legal_principle: The state’s 1934 Regulation and 1939 Constitution preserved the ruler’s plenary powers. Following the lapse of British paramountcy, those powers continued, subject to the agreements saved by section 7 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947. The Instrument of Accession preserved the ruler’s sovereignty and powers except as provided by that instrument. An absolute ruler could authorize another person to exercise all the ruler’s powers; the Court relied on Re Delhi Laws Act, 1912, [1951] SCR 747, for the principle that a sovereign authority may confer its powers on another.

rule.if: enactment_validity_challenge and ruler_had_plenary_governing_powers and ruler_transferred_all_government_functions and transfer_remained_in_force

predicates.enactment_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of an enactment in a court proceeding.
predicates.ruler_had_plenary_governing_powers: The ruler held the legislative, executive, and judicial powers concerning the government of the state.
predicates.ruler_transferred_all_government_functio: The ruler entrusted another person with all governing powers, including the power to make laws.
predicates.transfer_remained_in_force: The transfer of governing powers had not been revoked when the enactment was made.

issues.definition: When a challenge to an enactment concerns a person exercising powers transferred by a ruler with plenary governing powers, and the transfer remains in force, the person has authority to enact the law.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional arrangements then applicable to the state did not remove the ruler’s plenary legislative powers before the state’s constituent assembly determined its constitutional form of government.
material_facts: The ruler’s proclamation adopting the forthcoming Constitution of India to the extent applicable did not purport to alter the authority previously transferred to the delegate.
Only specified provisions of the Indian Constitution were applied to the state, and the provisions governing the general structure of state governments and the legislative lists were not applied.
The constitutional relationship between the state and India was to be finally determined by the state’s Constituent Assembly, which had not yet made its decision when the challenged law was enacted.
issues.conclusion: The application of the specified Indian constitutional provisions, including Article 370, did not limit the delegate’s plenary legislative powers when the law was enacted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Article 370 as a temporary arrangement intended to leave the ultimate constitutional relationship to the state’s Constituent Assembly. It held that Article 370 and the specified constitutional provisions could not, by implication, limit the ruler’s plenary legislative powers preserved by the state’s Constitution and the Instrument of Accession. The Court also treated the initial application of Article 385 and certain legislative provisions as formal or notional where they did not alter the state’s constitutional position.

predicates.enactment_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of an enactment in a court proceeding.
predicates.constitutional_arrangement_left_state_go: The constitutional arrangement left the final form of the state’s government to a future decision by its constituent assembly.
predicates.general_state_government_provisions_not_: The constitutional provisions that would otherwise have established the general structure of state government were not applied to the state.
predicates.ruler_had_plenary_governing_powers: The ruler held the legislative, executive, and judicial powers concerning the government of the state.

issues.definition: If a validity challenge concerns an enactment made while the state’s government form remained unsettled, the general state-government provisions had not been applied, and the ruler held plenary governing powers, the constitutional arrangement did not remove that lawmaking power.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a final compensation award for land taken under the law did not invalidate the law where it provided for interim payments and no applicable constitutional compensation restriction barred its enactment.
material_facts: The law provided for an annuity to an expropriated proprietor until the state’s Constituent Assembly settled the question of compensation.
The constitutional provision invoked against the law had not been applied to the state when the law was enacted.
The law was subsequently treated as existing law and protected when the relevant constitutional provision was extended to the state.
issues.conclusion: The law was not invalid for failing to provide compensation in the form or amount sought by the challenger.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on section 26 of the law, which provided for interim annuities pending the Constituent Assembly’s decision. It held that Article 31 had not been applied to the state when the law was enacted; when the relevant property provision was later extended, the law was saved as existing law by the modified Article 31(5).
